# Preface {.unnumbered}

We use SQL to ask questions of tables, then use R to work with databases.
No R experience is needed for Part I. R users who know SQL: start at Part II.

```{r fig.align='center', echo=FALSE, out.width="60%"}
knitr::include_graphics('img/rdbsql.png')
```

## Structure of the book {.unnumbered}

**Part I: SQL** is the SQL-first companion to the free
[Intro to SQL course]({{< var sql_course_url >}}). We start with databases,
tables and queries in @sec-sql-intro. We select, sort and filter rows in
@sec-sqlbasics, summarise groups in @sec-sql2, and combine tables in @sec-joins.
We use public flight data from **nycflights13**. The SQL examples run directly
against SQLite, and the book shows their results.

The full Part I outline reserves chapters 3, 5 and 7 for calculated columns
and SQLite types, missing values, and where SQL goes next. These chapters
are planned; the current navigation contains the available chapters only.

**Part II: SQL from R** starts with **DBI** in @sec-dbi and **dbplyr** in
@sec-dbplyr, including joins with dplyr verbs. The production and DuckDB
chapters follow. These chapters show how to connect, send queries and bring
results into R. Their existing examples use their own data.

The cheatsheet is an appendix. The [one-page DBI cheatsheet](cheatsheet/dbi-cheatsheet.pdf)
is also available for R users. The existing Part II scripts live in `code/`;
@sec-sql-intro explains how to build the Part I database and follow along.

## Software information {.unnumbered}

The R session information when compiling this book is shown below:

```{r session}
sessionInfo()
```

We do not add prompts (`>` and `+`) to R source code in this book, and we comment out the text output with two hashes `##` by default, as you can see from the R session information above. This is for your convenience when you want to copy and run the code (the text output will be ignored since it is commented out). Package names are in bold text (e.g., **rmarkdown**), and function names are followed by parentheses (e.g., `bookdown::render_book()`). The double-colon operator `::` means accessing an object from a package.
